## How I predicted SHG from structure

**Symmetry first.** SHG vanishes by symmetry in centrosymmetric crystals, so that's the primary physical gate. I checked all structures with spglib: every one of the 200 training materials *and* all 100 candidates is non-centrosymmetric. So symmetry doesn't separate the pool — this is a curated NLO set, and I need to predict *magnitude*, not just presence.

**Magnitude physics.** The largest lever on |d_ij| is the band gap (Miller's rule: χ⁽²⁾ scales roughly inversely with gap), which for these materials tracks anion chemistry and bond ionicity. I engineered structure- and composition-based features capturing this: electronegativity spread (ionicity/gap proxy), anion type fractions (chalcogenide vs. halide vs. oxide), atomic polarizabilities, packing/density, distortive-cation flags (d⁰ and ns² lone-pair cations), and point-group/polarity descriptors.

The feature importances validated the physics: **electronegativity spread and range dominate**, followed by halide fraction and minimum anion electronegativity. Ionic fluorides/oxides (large EN spread, wide gap) sit at low |d_ij|; covalent chalcogenides (small EN spread, narrow gap) sit high — exactly the expected trend.

**Model.** I regressed log₁₀|d_ij| (the target spans 0.01–302 pm/V) using a variance-reduced ensemble of Random Forest, Extra Trees, and Gradient Boosting across multiple seeds. Repeated 5-fold CV gave log₁₀ RMSE ≈ 0.42 vs. 0.69 baseline — i.e. typical predictions land within ~2.5× of truth, honest for structure-only SHG. The pool sits fully inside the training feature ranges (no extrapolation), and predicted medians match the training median (~15 pm/V), indicating good calibration.
